chief_complaint: episodic pounding headache, sweating, and palpitations
hpi_details: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with episodic pounding headache, sweating, and palpitations. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his sudden pounding heart and cold sweats are severe panic attacks triggered by stressful deadlines at work.
concerns: He is worried that these pounding episodes will trigger a fatal heart attack or stroke while he is home alone.
expectations: He hopes to get an ECG done today and a prescription for a fast-acting sedative or heart pill to stop the pounding spells when they hit.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pheochromocytoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Biochemical confirmation with plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines precedes anatomic imaging and surgery; alpha-blockade followed by beta-blockade is used only as preoperative preparation after a catecholamine-secreting tumor is confirmed.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pheochromocytoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Anxiety disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe hypertension during episodes.
management_principles: Obtain plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines, localize a confirmed tumor with imaging, then arrange specialist preoperative alpha-blockade followed by beta-blockade when needed before surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

history.answer: For the past few weeks, I have been getting these sudden spells where my head pounds intensely, I break out in heavy sweat, and my heart starts racing in my chest.
The spells began out of the blue about a month ago. They have become noticeably more frequent and intense lately, and I have been feeling completely worn out and fatigued.
Each episode strikes suddenly and reaches maximum intensity within a minute or two. It is not an ongoing ache; it hits all at once like a storm.
They used to happen once or twice a week, but now they occur every two or three days. Each attack usually lasts about fifteen to thirty minutes before gradually fading.
The throbbing is severe and affects my entire head, though I feel the pounding most intensely across my forehead and the top of my skull.
It is a violent, pulsating pounding sensation. During the worst of it, the pain is easily an eight or nine out of ten.
Sometimes bending over, sudden physical exertion, or emotional stress at work seems to trigger an episode, but other times it strikes while I am just resting quietly.
Nothing really cuts the spell short once it begins. Sitting completely still and taking slow breaths helps me endure it until it subsides on its own.
I checked my blood pressure at a pharmacy kiosk during one of these attacks last week, and the machine read over 190 on top. I was shocked because I have never had high numbers before.
No, I do not get any warning flashes, zigzag lines, or blind spots before the pounding starts.
I feel mildly nauseated and queasy when my heart pounds so fast, but I have not thrown up, and bright lights or loud sounds do not bother me.
No, I have not noticed any eye redness, tearing, runny nose, or drooping of my eyelids during the attacks.
No fever or chills at all, though I break out in a drenching cold sweat during every attack.
No, my neck is not stiff at all, and I can move my head in any direction without pain.
No, I have not had any weakness in my arms or legs, numbness, slurred speech, confusion, or seizures.
My eyesight stays normal throughout. I have not experienced blurry vision, double vision, or pain behind my eyes.
No, my temples are not tender to touch, my jaw does not ache when I chew, and my shoulders and hips feel completely normal.
No, I have not bumped my head, fallen, or had any recent injuries.
I tried taking over-the-counter acetaminophen a few times when an attack started, but it did not help the pounding at all, so I stopped taking it.
No, our home uses central electric heating, and my wife has felt completely healthy with no headaches whatsoever.
No, I have never had cancer, tumors, or any immune deficiency conditions.
My health has always been unremarkable, with no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, or kidney problems.
I had my appendix removed when I was eighteen, but I have had no other operations or hospital stays since.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal remedies.
I have no allergies to any medicines, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or nicotine products.
I drink one or two glasses of beer socially on the weekend, but nothing more than that.
I work full-time as an office administrator, and I live comfortably at home with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure in his late sixties. Nobody in my family has had adrenal tumors, thyroid tumors, or early unexplained heart problems.
I thought I was just having severe panic attacks or drinking way too much coffee when deadlines pile up.
I'm terrified that my heart is going to give out and I'll have a fatal heart attack while I'm alone in the house.
I'm hoping you can check my heart with an ECG today and give me something to stop these terrifying pounding spells.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and temperature is 36.7 degrees Celsius.
Middle-aged man sitting comfortably on the examination table, appearing mildly fatigued with cool, slightly moist palms, but in no acute respiratory distress.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; visual fields are intact to confrontation, and funduscopic examination reveals sharp optic disc margins with no papilledema or retinal hemorrhages.
No tenderness elicited on palpation or percussion over the frontal and maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
Neck is completely supple with full passive range of motion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are both negative.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial movements, intact palate elevation, and normal extraocular movements.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength across all major muscle groups in the upper and lower extremities bilaterally.
Intact sensation to light touch and pinprick throughout all dermatomes without focal sensory deficit.
Finger-to-nose testing is accurate bilaterally, rapid alternating movements are intact, and casual gait is stable and balanced.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs appreciated.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended without palpable mass or organomegaly; gentle deep palpation precipitates no sudden symptom surge or pain.
Mild fine postural tremor noted when arms and fingers are outstretched bilaterally.
